title: A time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
hookLine: a time to be born, to die, to weep, to laugh, to keep silence

cards: You may know this passage without knowing you know it. It's read at funerals and at weddings.
In 1965 a rock band took it to the top of the American charts, in a song Pete Seeger had set almost word for word from the King James Bible, adding only a refrain and a few words at the end.
And it comes from Ecclesiastes, from the Preacher who just told us everything is breath.

teach.h: TO EVERY THING THERE IS A SEASON.
teach.b: It starts with a heading: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Then the list, in pairs.
"A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted." A time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance.
And a line for every hard conversation: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak."

There are fourteen pairs, twenty-eight times, and every pair holds two opposites. That's the shape of a life: not one long mood, but a back and forth. The Preacher isn't telling you to pick the nice half.
He says both have their time. Grief isn't a failure of joy. Silence isn't a failure of speech.
The question is never which feeling is right, but which time it is now. Readers hear this in two keys. For some it's comfort: whatever you're going through is a season, and seasons turn.
For others it's sobering, because the Preacher goes straight on to ask what anyone gains from all this toil, since the times come whether we like them or not. Then a strange line.

teach.h: THE EVERLASTING SET IN THE HEART.
teach.b: The King James says God has set the world in their heart; the Hebrew word, olam, can also mean the everlasting. And yet no one can find out the whole of what God has done. We live inside the seasons.
We can't see the whole calendar.

teach.h: A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE, AND A TIME TO SPEAK.
teach.b: This week ran from Job's ending through wisdom's beginning, the ant, rakh, eshet chayil and all is breath, to a time for everything.

how: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 is often read at Christian funerals, and it is also read at weddings, graduations and memorial services, often by a family member.

games.q: what's inside the list — tap the pairs.

s: the Preacher tells us to choose laughing over weeping
he says both have their time. grief isn't a failure of joy.
a 1960s hit song took its words almost straight from the King James Bible
Pete Seeger set the passage nearly word for word, adding a refrain.
the passage says we can see the whole of what God has done
it says the everlasting, olam, is set in the heart, yet no one can find out the whole of God's work.

games.q: you're in a season of grief. a friend tells you it's time to cheer up. what does the Preacher's list say?
o: your friend is right: laughing is better than weeping.
there is a time to mourn, and this may be it.
games.why: "a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance." the list never ranks the halves. each has its season, and seasons turn.

practice: Let the list play slowly through your mind, a time to plant, a time to weep, a time to laugh, a time to keep silence, a time to speak, and notice which line catches.
Don't pick the one you wish were true; name the one that is, plainly: it's a time to mourn, or a time to build. If you pray, offer that season to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Et. Hebrew for a fitting moment, said twenty-eight times in the Preacher's list: every season of a life, the hard half and the easy half, each in its time.

orig.note: Hebrew: a time, a fitting moment. it appears twenty-eight times in the list.

carryVoice: Your line: a time to speak. And, just as surely, a time to keep silence. See you tomorrow.
